opus-5.5.text:
I think the potential is enormous, and honestly I'd argue it's one of the most underappreciated directions right now. If you look at how progress actually happens in science, it's not a single optimizer climbing toward a fixed objective. It's a population of ideas, many of them dead ends, some of which turn out to be stepping stones to something nobody could have anticipated. Evolutionary search captures that dynamic in a way that standard gradient-based optimization against a fixed benchmark just doesn't.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that we now have foundation models that can act as really powerful mutation and selection operators. In classic genetic programming you were mutating syntax trees more or less at random, and the search space was so vast that you rarely found anything interesting. Now you can have a large language model propose a meaningful variation of a program, a proof sketch, or a research idea, because it has absorbed so much human knowledge about what tends to be interesting and what tends to work. And you can use models to judge interestingness too, which was always the hard part of open-endedness. We had a paper called OMNI that leaned on exactly this idea: using models of human notions of interestingness to decide what to explore next.

In domains like math and computer science you have a big advantage, which is verifiability. You can run the code, you can check the proof, you can measure the speed of an algorithm. That gives you a grounded signal, so the system can't just hallucinate its way to progress. Systems like FunSearch and AlphaEvolve have shown you can discover genuinely new constructions and faster algorithms this way, things that weren't in the training data. That's really the key point for me: it's a way of getting beyond the data rather than just interpolating it.

AI research itself is where it gets really exciting, and a bit harder. There the evaluation is more expensive and fuzzier. What counts as a good research contribution? But we're starting to see systems that propose hypotheses, write experiment code, run it, and archive the results so future generations can build on them. The archive is crucial. Keeping a growing library of diverse, interesting artifacts, not just the current best, is what lets you find those stepping stones.

The open challenges I'd point to are: how to keep generating novelty without collapsing onto what the base model already finds likely, how to define interestingness robustly so the system doesn't game it, and how to scale evaluation. And of course there are safety questions once these systems start improving the very AI systems doing the search. But overall I'm quite optimistic. I think open-ended, evolutionary approaches powered by foundation models could be a core ingredient in getting to systems that make genuine scientific discoveries, and maybe in accelerating AI research itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really one of the most exciting directions right now. If you look at what evolutionary methods have historically been good at, it's exploring vast search spaces where you don't have a nice gradient to follow, where the objective is deceptive or sparse, and where you benefit from maintaining diversity rather than collapsing onto a single solution. And for a long time the bottleneck was that the mutation and crossover operators were essentially random. You'd flip some bits, you'd swap some subtrees in a program, and most of what you got back was garbage. So the search was very sample-inefficient.

What's changed is that we now have language models that have absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge about code, about mathematics, about how research is actually done. And so you can use them as a very intelligent mutation operator. Instead of random perturbations, you ask the model, here's a program, here's how it performed, here's a related program that did something interesting, propose a variation. And suddenly the search is operating in a much more semantically meaningful space. That's really the insight behind things like FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, and in our own work on things like Prompt Breeder and the DiscoPOP work where we evolved preference optimization losses, and more recently the AI Scientist line of work, where you're treating the research process itself as something you can search over.

Why I think the open-ended framing matters so much in computer science, math, and AI research specifically is that these are domains where we don't actually know what the right objective is in advance. Math isn't about optimizing one fixed function. It's about discovering interesting structure, generating new conjectures, finding problems that are at the right level of difficulty to be learnable. And that's exactly what open-ended algorithms like novelty search, MAP-Elites, POET, and so on are designed to do. They're not just climbing a hill, they're building an ever-growing archive of stepping stones, and the stepping stones that turn out to matter are often ones you would never have selected for directly.

And then there's this very appealing property that these domains are verifiable. If you evolve a sorting algorithm or a matrix multiplication kernel, you can run it and check. If you evolve a proof, you can send it through Lean. If you evolve a new training recipe, you can actually train the model and measure it. So you get a grounded fitness signal, which means the language model's hallucinations get filtered out by reality rather than accumulating. That's the combination I'm most excited about, the creativity and prior knowledge of the model paired with the rigor of an external verifier and the exploratory pressure of an open-ended search process.

I'd be honest that there are real challenges. Compute cost is one, because every evaluation might mean training a model or running an expensive simulation. And the harder question is how you measure interestingness in a way that doesn't just collapse into whatever the language model already thinks is interesting, because then you're just rediscovering the training distribution. We've been playing with having the model itself act as a judge of novelty, and it works surprisingly well, but it's not fully solved. Still, if you ask me where I think genuinely new scientific knowledge is going to come out of AI systems first, I'd bet on this kind of setup, open-ended evolutionary search driven by foundation models in verifiable domains, rather than on a single model just being prompted to be clever.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s enormous potential, particularly in domains where we can automatically evaluate whether something works. In computer science, you can run a program, test it, measure its performance. In mathematics, if you’re working within a formal system, you can check a proof. That gives you a feedback signal for search, even when you don’t know how to construct the solution yourself.

The exciting thing about combining evolutionary search with large language models is that you can make the variation much more informed. Instead of randomly changing a program, a model can propose a meaningful modification, or bring together ideas from different candidate solutions. You can then test those proposals and use the results to guide further exploration.

But I think the open-ended aspect is the really important challenge. If you optimize against one fixed benchmark, you may get very good at that benchmark without discovering anything fundamentally new. How do you maintain diversity? How do you preserve ideas that aren’t immediately useful but might become stepping stones? And can the system discover new problems worth solving, alongside new solutions?

For AI research, that could eventually mean systems that propose an algorithm, implement it, run experiments, and build on what they learn. There’s a lot to get right there, especially around evaluation and computational cost. But the prospect of having a process that keeps generating useful discoveries, rather than converging on a single answer, is very exciting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s enormous potential, particularly in domains where you can automatically check whether something works. In computer science, you can run a program and test it. In mathematics, if you’re working with a formal system, you can check a proof. That gives you a feedback signal for search, even when discovering the solution is extremely difficult.

What’s exciting is combining that with models that can propose useful variations. Rather than making random changes to a program, you can have a model suggest a different algorithm, explain a hypothesis, or generate a new experiment. Evolutionary search then gives you a way to maintain a population of ideas, test them, and build on the ones that are promising.

But the open-ended part is crucial. If you optimize against one fixed benchmark, you may get very good at that benchmark without discovering anything fundamentally new. For research, we need systems that can explore different directions and perhaps help generate the problems themselves. And that raises a difficult question: how do you recognize an interesting stepping stone before you know where it leads?

So I’m optimistic, but I don’t think it’s just a matter of putting a language model inside an evolutionary loop. The evaluation, the diversity of the search, and the environment in which those ideas can develop are all going to matter enormously.
